titre: The Summer Artificial Intelligence Got Its Name
accroche: In 1955, four researchers drafted a grant request for a summer of work at Dartmouth. The word they coined there outlived their project.
contenu_vulgarise:
On August 31, 1955, John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester, and Claude Shannon signed a funding request addressed to the Rockefeller Foundation. In it, they proposed bringing together, the following summer at Dartmouth College in Hanover, New Hampshire, about ten researchers around a single idea: every aspect of learning, or any other feature of intelligence, can in principle be described precisely enough for a machine to simulate it.

## A name chosen for its neutrality

It is in this document that the four authors use the phrase "artificial intelligence" to describe this research program. McCarthy preferred it to already-taken labels, such as Norbert Wiener's cybernetics, partly because it belonged to no one yet and tied the workshop to no existing school of thought. The phrase first served as a convenient label for a grant request; it would go on to name an entire field of research.

## A gathering more modest than its name suggests

The workshop ran from June 18 to August 17, 1956, roughly eight weeks, even though the proposal had spoken of a two-month study. Eleven participants were announced at the outset, including Allen Newell and Herbert Simon, who came to present a program capable of proving logic theorems. But notes taken on site by one of the attendees, mathematician Ray Solomonoff, make it possible to reconstruct a list of about twenty names in all: researchers came, left, and came back depending on their availability that summer. Only three of them, Solomonoff, Minsky, and McCarthy, stayed from the first day to the last, and the daily sessions drew, according to those same notes, only between three and eight people.

## What the workshop actually produced

The gathering did not deliver the intelligent machine promised in the grant request, which had aimed to get machines to use language, form abstractions, and improve themselves: no major scientific result came out of it directly. What it mainly did was put, in the same room, for a few weeks of a scattered summer, the researchers who would go on to found the field for decades to come, and gave them a shared name to gather under. Some historians of science retroactively nickname it "the Constitutional Convention of artificial intelligence," a label that lends this informal, loosely attended gathering more solemnity than it had at the time. The name, for its part, has largely outlived the forgotten details of that summer.

carte.punch: The phrase "artificial intelligence" was born in a 1955 grant request.
carte.idee: John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester, and Claude Shannon coined the term to describe a summer workshop at Dartmouth, in 1956. The gathering itself drew, on any given day, only a handful of researchers with fluctuating attendance.

quiz.question: What sets the actual course of the 1956 Dartmouth workshop apart from the image often kept of it?
choix: It was held not at Dartmouth but at the Rockefeller Foundation's headquarters
The daily sessions drew only between three and eight people, with fluctuating attendance
None of the four authors of the 1955 proposal attended the workshop
The workshop lasted two years instead of the two months announced in the proposal
quiz.explication: Ray Solomonoff's notes show that about twenty researchers passed through over the summer, but that the daily sessions drew, in practice, only between three and eight people, far from the image of a founding congress with everyone present the whole time.
